transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

Um… I guess it’s mostly work stuff. In longer sales strategy meetings, I keep finding reasons to get up when I’m supposed to just stay seated—like refilling my water or walking over by the printer for a minute. It’s been happening enough that I thought I should probably talk to someone.
Have you noticed this kind of restlessness and urge to get up and move around since you were a child or teenager, or is this something that's only started more recently?

I think it’s been around a long time. Like, even before high school… I remember elementary school teachers writing things like I was bright, but I rushed, talked out of turn, forgot homework, and my desk was always full of half-finished papers. So… not just recent, I guess.

When you notice this urge to get up and move, is it usually accompanied by a specific worry or fear running through your mind, or does it feel more like just needing to move without a particular worried thought attached?

It’s not really a specific fear, I don’t think. It’s more just… I feel like I need to move. Like in those long strategy meetings, I’ll get up to refill water or stand near the printer for a bit, even though I know I’m supposed to stay seated.
These days, do you still notice trouble staying focused on tasks, losing track of things, or forgetting important details, similar to what happened in school?

Yeah… some. In longer strategy meetings, or if I’m reading a client brief, I’ll start out paying attention, but then a few minutes later I realize I’ve just been staring at the same slide or paragraph and I don’t really know what I just read or what the last point was.
Do you notice this same kind of restlessness or trouble focusing outside of work, like at home or in your personal relationships?
I’m not really sure. I mean… probably a little, but I don’t pay as much attention to it at home. It’s less obvious than at work, I guess.
Can you give me a specific example of a time at home or with family/friends when you noticed yourself losing focus or needing to move around, similar to what happens at work?

I guess the clearest example is still more at work, honestly. Like the long sales strategy meetings… I know I’m supposed to stay seated, but I’ll keep getting up to refill water or kind of pace near the printer. At home, I can’t think of a specific one as easily.

Thinking about situations outside of work, like managing finances, driving, or completing household chores/errands, have you noticed similar problems with restlessness or losing focus that have caused any actual trouble, like forgetting bills or getting distracted while driving?

Um… not really that I can think of. I mean, I might forget little things here and there, but nothing like missed bills or anything serious with driving. Household stuff is just… normal procrastination, I guess. I haven’t noticed a clear problem outside of work.
Do you notice yourself interrupting others, blurting out responses, or feeling impatient waiting your turn in conversations or situations like waiting in line, outside of work?

Yeah… maybe sometimes. If someone’s going through a deck and I think of something, I’ll kind of jump in or go over to add it, even if it probably could’ve waited. I don’t think I’m trying to be rude, it just feels like I should say it before I lose it.
Can you think of a specific time with friends or family—like during a conversation or group activity—when you interrupted someone or blurted something out before they finished?

Not really with family or friends that I can pin down. The example I keep thinking of is at work—if someone’s going through a deck and I have an idea, I’ll kind of pop over or cut in to add it, even though it probably could’ve waited.

Do you notice a similar pattern when you're doing something for yourself outside of work—like reading a book, watching a movie, or pursuing a hobby—where you find your mind drifting or you lose track of what you were doing?

Yeah… I guess with reading more than hobbies. Like if I’m reading a client brief or something kind of dense, I’ll start out paying attention, and then a few minutes later I’m just staring at the same paragraph and realize I don’t really know what I just read. It’s not every time, but it happens.

Can you think of a specific time during a leisure activity—like watching a movie, having dinner with friends, or attending a social event—when you felt restless or had trouble staying focused, similar to what happens at work?

I’m not sure I can think of a clear social example. It’s more like… in longer strategy meetings, or if I’m reading a client brief, I’ll start off focused and then realize I’ve been staring at the same slide or paragraph and I don’t actually know what the last point was.
Has anyone close to you—like a partner, roommate, or family member—ever commented that you seem restless, distracted, or forgetful at home, even if you haven't noticed it yourself?
Not that I can think of. I mean, no one’s really said that to me directly at home. Maybe little comments here and there, but nothing that stands out.
Has your restlessness, difficulty focusing, or blurting out ideas at work ever led to any real consequences—like a supervisor commenting on it, a missed deadline, or a performance review issue?

Yeah… a little. It’s come up in performance reviews, kind of framed as needing to be more consistent or careful with follow-through. And there was one client complaint that really bothered me. I don’t want to get into all the details, but it made me worry that if I’m not more on top of it, I could hurt the account’s trust in me, even though I do care a lot about doing the work well.

Going back further, during college or any other schooling, did professors or classmates ever comment on similar restlessness, distractibility, or impulsivity that actually affected your grades or performance?

Yeah… I think so. Not so much college that I remember clearly, but even earlier. In elementary school, teachers would write things like I was bright but rushed through work, talked out of turn, forgot homework, or had a messy desk full of half-finished papers. I guess it was kind of the same pattern, just… school version.

When you're at home doing something relatively passive, like watching TV or sitting through a long meal, do you notice yourself fidgeting, needing to get up, or feeling restless in the same way you do during work meetings?

At home, not as much that I notice. The thing that really made me come in is more at work—like in long sales strategy meetings, I keep getting up when I know I’m supposed to stay seated. I’ll say I’m refilling water or go pace by the printer for a minute. It’s… hard to just sit there.

patient.answer: Yeah… a little. It’s come up in performance reviews, kind of framed as needing to be more consistent or careful with follow-through. And there was one client complaint that really bothered me. I don’t want to get into all the details, but it made me worry that if I’m not more on top of it, I could hurt the account’s trust in me, even though I do care a lot about doing the work well.

inference.note: Confirmation of real-world impairment at work (performance review issues, client complaint) strengthens support for ADHD, though cross-setting impairment outside work remains only mildly endorsed. No new differential diagnoses emerged; F90.0 remains the leading candidate.

doctor.intent: Determine whether functional impairment from these symptoms also occurred in another setting (e.g., college/school or personal relationships) to confirm cross-setting impairment required for ADHD diagnosis
doctor.question: Going back further, during college or any other schooling, did professors or classmates ever comment on similar restlessness, distractibility, or impulsivity that actually affected your grades or performance?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: I remember this starting way before high school—my elementary school teachers wrote that I was bright but rushed, talked out of turn, forgot homework, and had a desk stuffed with half-finished papers.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about whether similar ADHD-related symptoms were present earlier during schooling, which most directly relates to historical onset of symptoms before adulthood.

patient.answer: Yeah… I think so. Not so much college that I remember clearly, but even earlier. In elementary school, teachers would write things like I was bright but rushed through work, talked out of turn, forgot homework, or had a messy desk full of half-finished papers. I guess it was kind of the same pattern, just… school version.

inference.note: Childhood history (elementary school) now clearly corroborates cross-situational impairment, satisfying the multi-setting criterion via retrospective evidence even though current symptoms are most prominent at work. Both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (restlessness/pacing, blurting ideas, distractibility) are present, so combined presentation (F90.2) is added alongside inattentive-predominant (F90.0) pending final symptom count clarification.

doctor.intent: Determine whether hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (not just inattentiveness) are present and impairing in a non-work setting, which is needed to distinguish combined-type ADHD from predominantly inattentive ADHD.
doctor.question: When you're at home doing something relatively passive, like watching TV or sitting through a long meal, do you notice yourself fidgeting, needing to get up, or feeling restless in the same way you do during work meetings?

target_item.name: Leaving_Seat
target_item.manifestation: Honestly, what made me come in is that I keep getting up during long sales strategy meetings when I know I’m supposed to stay seated, even if it’s just to refill water or pace by the printer.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether I need to get up or feel unable to stay seated during passive situations, which most directly matches leaving my seat when remaining seated is expected.

patient.answer: At home, not as much that I notice. The thing that really made me come in is more at work—like in long sales strategy meetings, I keep getting up when I know I’m supposed to stay seated. I’ll say I’m refilling water or go pace by the printer for a minute. It’s… hard to just sit there.

inference.note: Symptoms remain cross-situational in origin (childhood history) but predominantly reported in work settings; inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms both persist, keeping combined presentation (F90.2) and inattentive-predominant (F90.0) as candidates. No new information rules out either subtype.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient demonstrates a long-standing (since elementary school) pattern of both inattentive symptoms (losing focus while reading/reviewing briefs, disorganization with notes scattered across multiple platforms, forgetting homework as a child, difficulty with follow-through) and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (persistent urge to get up during meetings, pacing, interrupting/blurting out ideas during presentations). Symptoms are not driven by anxious worry (patient explicitly denies a specific fear accompanying the restlessness), making generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1) less likely. Symptoms are present in both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive domains rather than inattentive symptoms alone, arguing against F90.0. Functional impairment is clearly documented at work (performance review feedback, client complaint) and impairment was historically present in childhood schooling, supporting onset prior to age 12. Cross-setting pervasiveness is less robustly documented (patient reports difficulty mainly recognizing symptoms at work, with vague/uncertain report of symptoms at home), which is a limitation, but the childhood documentation across school settings and clear impairment in current major life domain (occupational) support the diagnosis of ADHD, combined presentation.
